subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-POSSIBILITY OF COMPENSATORY PAYMENTS TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-POSSIBILITY OF COMPENSATORY PAYMENTS TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was a little more than a week ago that I put a question to the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) concerning the problem he was having reaching an agreement for the use of the RCMP forces in eight of our provinces. The suggestion I made to him in the question was that he might conclude an agreement with all ten of the provinces so that the two largest provinces, Ontario and my own province of Quebec, which use their own police forces, could receive compensatory payments in lieu of the benefits which are received by the other provinces.
This question derives from some questions I have been putting to the various solicitors general and also on the order paper for the last several years suggesting that if there are benefits accruing to the other provinces from the use of the RCMP and since there is a contribution made by the taxpayers in the two largest provinces of Ontario and Quebec, there should be compensatory payments in lieu of the benefits received by the other provinces.
In his reply, the Solicitor General stated that it is not intended to be a cost-sharing agreement and never has been. Maybe, but the figures might illustrate otherwise. The latest figures I have, given to me by a predecessor of the present Solicitor General, indicate that there are approximately 2,500 members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec obviously being used for federal duties or federal purposes. Of the approximately 8,200 members of the RCMP in the other eight provinces, approximately 2,100 are used for federal purposes, 4,100 for provincial purposes and 2,000 for municipal duties.
In addition, I am told that the amount charged to the eight provinces in the last year for which figures appear to be available-the 1979-80 period-totalled SI 19 million.
Going back some five years to 1975-76, the charge in that period was $68 million. I was only able to do my arithmetic for that particular year because of comparable figures, but the calculation, based on the number of personnel of the RCMP used in that year divided into the $68 million charged, indicated that we were charging at that time some $11,000 per person.
From that figure I gained the impression that this was a concessionary rate, and thus I suggested that if in order to maintain one police force in the eight provinces we were in effect to charge only to the eight provinces a rate somewhat lower-in fact, possibly substantially lower-than the actual cost to the federal government of those persons employed and since this cost was paid in part by the taxes of the residents of the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec, the two provinces which have two-thirds of the population of this country, there should be some return to these two provinces to compensate for the benefit which was being received in the other eight provinces.
April 13, 1981

I think it is important at this time to stress this point because the eight provinces, which are apparently reluctant to conclude an agreement, are under the impression-apparently also-that the federal government should be making some contribution toward the cost of the police forces, the RCMP, which are being used in these eight provinces. If this is to continue to be the case, the taxpayers of the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec should be compensated for whatever benefits are being given in these eight other provinces. Alternatively, the Solicitor General should ensure that the amount being charged is fair and just, so that there is no cost to the taxpayers in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-POSSIBILITY OF COMPENSATORY PAYMENTS TO ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) raised in his question a subject which at the moment is my greatest priority as Solicitor General. That is the renegotiation of the contracts for provincial policing services between Canada and eight provinces and 180 odd municipalities across the country. Those contracts expired last Tuesday. They are a very important job for the RCMP. In fact, almost half of the RCMP are engaged in providing provincial and municipal police services.
In their federal role, and there are 11,000 of them across the country doing federal policing, all of the payments of course come from the national taxpayers and the national treasury, as they should. However, under the provincial and municipal role where we provide police to fulfil the responsibilities to other levels of government, we expect that those governments and their constituents who benefit from these services will pay the largest share of the cost for those services.
The hon. member indicated that we should not charge those provinces any less than the cost of the service. I disagree. I think we should charge less than the services cost because there is some national benefit from having the RCMP as a provincial police force and a municipal police force. There are efficiencies. The country benefits from having the same police force working at three levels; sharing their training, communications facilities, offices and other facilities. These are advantages from which the provinces should benefit.
At the same time, these highly trained members of the RCMP are competent when they are working at the municipal level and provincial level to help us in the federal policing program. We are prepared to recognize that benefit and contribute a share of that cost to the provinces and municipalities. The question is how much.
We want to share with the provinces the cost to such an extent that the federal taxpayer will not be subsidizing these provincial police services. The hon. member for Vaudreuil is correct when he states there would be no justification for the federal government providing a subsidy to those provinces.
We do not intend to provide a subsidy. We provide policing service. The offer was available to Ontario and Quebec, not to get money from the federal government, and Canada would have benefited from it, but to have the RCMP serving in their provinces as provincial and municipal police. They chose, as is their constitutional right, to do the policing themselves.
Adjournment Debate
Those provinces which use the force benefit from it. However, the benefits are in policing. The benefits should not be in some subsidy from fellow taxpayers at the national level to those who are in municipalities, whether or not they pay for their own policing, or who are in provinces which do not have the benefit of the RCMP.
These contracts are now up for negotiation. We have not settled the price. However, the principle is very clear. Each level of government will only be expected to pay for the benefits it receives. I hope to be able to report shortly to the House that contracts have been renegotiated and that the RCMP will continue to perform that very valued and historic role for the provinces and municipalities.

subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-RE-OPENING OF CONTRACT TO CONSTRUCT F-18 FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
SUPPLY AND SERVICES-RE-OPENING OF CONTRACT TO CONSTRUCT F-18 FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight at 10.19 to discuss the plight of over 1,000 workers who have been laid off at McDonnell Douglas (Canada) and the mysterious situation surrounding the F-18 contract signed between this government and McDonnell Douglas of St. Louis for an amount in the area of $4 billion in 1981 dollars.
As the House knows, the Department of National Defence had been looking for a long time at various aircraft in order that a purchase be made to re-equip our armed forces which are using outdated equipment. Many in this House studied, through the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, the various proposals which were narrowed down to two: the F-16 and the F-18.
In meeting with McDonnell Douglas officials, I and many of my colleagues were assured that, if the Government of Canada awarded the fighter aircraft contract to McDonnell Douglas, the F-18 Hornet, the Canadian plant in Malton would receive a significant share of the Canadian offset program. At the same time, my colleague, Alex Jupp, the then member of Parliament for Mississauga North and I both tried to receive assurances that Orenda engines would get some of the work on the General Electric motors, but no assurances were given.
At the time the contract was to be announced, the Quebec Liberal caucus met with the makers of the F-16 which they favoured, not because it was the best for Canada, but because it promised more work for Quebec.
At the same time-and we can give them full marks-they meet with McDonnell Douglas. What went on at that latter meeting has not been told. Was the Quebec Liberal caucus promised additional work in Quebec to the detriment of Ontario? Did the Quebec caucus support the F-18 contract because of a deal which was made between them and McDonnell Douglas? When asked that question, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) refused to answer, as can be seen at page 9103 of Hansard for April 9.
The contract was awarded in Ottawa last spring by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne), and we were
9238

April 13, 1981
Adjournment Debate
all very excited. I attended the signing of the contract and was thrilled by the performance of the F-18 Hornet at the Ottawa International Airport. The workers at McDonnell Douglas were drinking champagne to celebrate, and now over 1,000 of them are walking the street looking for work.
Part of the offset program was construction of components or parts for the DC-9 and the DC-10. I would imagine that part of the contract has already been broken. McDonnell Douglas Canada, with the know-how and the trained manpower, bid on forward fuselage side panels and pylons for the new aircraft.
When Ottawa saw that there were no competing bids for side panels and pylons from Quebec, presto, a Crown corporation owned by the Government of Canada, located in Quebec, namely Canadair Ltd. put in its bid. In answer to a question which I posed on April 9, 1981, as found at page 9103 of Hansard, the Minister of Supply and Services said that it was an unsolicited bid. That is for the public to decide. Then the minister said:
-McDonnell Douglas invited the other bidders to attempt to fix their bids and the whole process is under review by McDonnell Douglas.
I would suggest that "fix their bids" is pretty strong language in the game of tendering, and begs more questions.
I submit that the F-18 contract has been a case of the worst kind of political pressure and that subcontractors in Ontario and their workers will be the victims. I cannot help but wonder, as to the workers at McDonnell Douglas, where the Onario Liberal caucus has been in Ottawa for the past year, especially the member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher).
When Bill Patrick, president of local 1967, United Auto Workers, which is the union that represents most of the workers at McDonnell Douglas, invited all political parties and Members of Parliament to a meeting with the union and its membership, not one Grit showed up. Not one Liberal was to be seen, not even the member for Mississauga North, which is where the meeting took place.
The Progressive Conservative Party was represented by the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and myself, the NDP was represented by Mike Cassidy, but there were no Liberals. Yet, some people wonder why the working man or woman or the unemployed, as most were at that meeting, are becoming so cynical at the complete inaction and non-interest the government displays. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), "Herb, lower the interest rates or I'll resign, Gray" has not lifted a finger to help. It takes Premier Davis to show the initiative, as he did last week, to travel to St. Louis to get some action, and there will be significant announcements made in the not-too-distant future. Union President Bill Patrick recognized this initiative as a positive step to help the workers with their plight.
What is happening with that multi-million dollar contract and the 2,000 new jobs promised, many of them at the McDonnell Douglas plant? Nothing to date. Why? The minister says the whole process is now under revision by McDonnell
Douglas. Why? Because the government asked them to change the process? I think it is time that the Liberal government came clean on the entire matter, levelled with the workers of McDonnell Douglas and with the people of Canada. What deals were made? What concessions were made to the Quebec caucus by McDonnell Douglas and/or the government? Finally, when, pray tell, can the sub-contract be expected to be signed so Canadians can start to work on the F-18? For every day that goes by, another F-18 and all its parts is being built in another country, and we lose.

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman Kelly (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-RE-OPENING OF CONTRACT TO CONSTRUCT F-18 FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to preface my remarks on behalf of the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) with two observations. First, although the CF-18 contract is very lengthy, it is a public document accessible to the hon. member opposite. It describes in great detail the large number of commitments that McDonnell Douglas has made to Canada in connection with the Hornet project. Two, the decision to purchase this particular aircraft was based not only on the sum of the contractual obligations it generated but, more important, because of the suitability of the aircraft itself for Canadian defence requirements.
As for the two questions asked by the hon. member on April 9, as reported at page 9103 of Hansard, I would first like to inform the House that McDonnell (Canada) was not the only firm to bid on the forward fuselage side panels and wing pylons when the bids closed the first time. An additional Canadian firm submitted a proposal to manufacture the forward side panels and two additional firms submitted proposals on the manufacture of the wing pylons.
I would also like to reiterate the minister's response to the second question, which may be found in Hansard on the same date and page I mentioned previously. That is to say that the government was not pressured, nor did it request McDonnell Douglas, St. Louis, to re-open tenders for any of the structural components. The company elected to solicit Canadian industry for new bids when Canadair expressed an interest to join in the competition. The government is not interested in interfering with the McDonnell Douglas normal bid solicitation process. It is not unusual for bids to be re-opened to seek additional tenders if the first bids received are not necessarily responsive to the requirements, or if the requirements change. It should be noted that escalation factors, exchange rates and production requirements have all changed to some extent since the tenders were first called. It is in this sense that the minister used the phrase "to fix" tenders. Perhaps he means "to update" tenders.
The government did not request a bid from Canadair on side panels, wing pylons or any other components. The government has an agreement to purchase complete CF-18 aircraft from McDonnell Douglas. That firm is responsible for choosing its suppliers according to its own policies and the applicable regulations and laws of the United States. In short, there is no assurance that any Canadian firm will be chosen to perform the work in question. Our contract requires that Canadian prices must be competitive with the cost of performing the
April 13, 1981

work in the United States. However, we have no reason to believe that this will not be the case. It is anticipated that McDonnell Douglas will identify the most attractive bidder within the next few weeks.
